title: New Zealand Inflation Eases in Q3
body: New Zealand's annual inflation rate eased to 3.7% in the third quarter of 2026, down from 4.1% in the previous quarter and slightly below market expectations of 3.8%. Despite this moderation, inflation remains above the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 1–3% target range. Petrol was the single largest contributor to annual inflation, surging 19.1% amid higher international oil and fuel prices linked to conflict in the Middle East. The cost of building new homes rose 3.2%, reflecting increased material, subcontractor, labour, and fuel costs. These rates, which are measured annually in the September quarter, have been a significant driver of inflation in recent years. On a quarterly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.7%, a marked slowdown from the 1.5% increase recorded in the second quarter. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6756 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

But what is driving that? Well, it's the thing we have been talking about every so often in the past two weeks, that being France's fiscal plight. And the worries are now growing rather quickly as French 10-year government bond yields have surged above 5%, hitting their highest levels since 2002. Besides that, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread is now widening towards a staggering 170 bps - its highest since 2011. It wasn't just too long ago that we were talking the line in the sand at 150 bps. All of a sudden, we're now nearly 20 bps up from that. The latest surge is another sign that investors are demanding a much higher premium to hold French debt, amid growing fiscal and political uncertainty. Looking at the EUR/CHF chart, we're already seeing some of those worries translate into price action. After all, France is Europe's second-largest economy and concerns there will have the potential to spill over into broader European assets and the euro.

title: France business confidence improves in October but cracks remain beneath the surface

title: Crude oil buyers remain in control from a technical perspective. What would tilt the bias lower?
body: Middle East risks keep oil supported Crude oil is moving back toward the $100 level today as Middle East risks give buyers another reason to push prices higher. In Adam's post, he outlines the bullish fundamental backdrop for oil: increased military risks involving the US and Israel, a continuing stalemate, and recent Houthi activity in Saudi Arabia adding to the anxiety. A war that was supposed to be quick and easy continues to drag on, keeping concerns about energy supplies firmly in play. The fundamental story is supportive. The technical price action is helping to confirm that story. The moving averages help tell the story Since bottoming on October 6 near $86.93—the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the July 2 low—crude oil has recovered above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, shown by the blue and green lines on the chart above. Those moving averages have since helped define support and keep the buyers in control. Initially, the 100-hour moving average provided support. More recently, sellers have managed to push below that faster-moving average, but the breaks have lacked follow-through. The rising 200-hour moving average has held, giving buyers a level to lean against before pushing the price back higher. That distinction is important for traders. A break below the 100-hour moving average gives sellers an opening. Holding above the 200-hour moving average keeps the buyers in play. To shift control, sellers need to break support and stay below it.

title: Trading Education: Gold falls despite lower yields: A lesson in trading what the market gives you
body: Gold typically benefits when Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar move lower. But "typically" is an important word. Those relationships can help frame an expectation. They do not guarantee the next move. Why do lower yields tend to support gold? Gold pays no interest. When bond yields fall, investors give up less income by owning gold instead of an interest-paying asset. Falling real yields—yields adjusted for inflation—are particularly supportive. A weaker dollar can also help. Gold is priced in dollars, so a declining greenback makes it less expensive for buyers using other currencies. When both move lower, gold can get a double tailwind. However, other forces can outweigh those benefits. A decline in the nominal Treasury yield alone also does not tell us what happened to real yields. Today provides an educational example. The U.S. 10-year yield is down around 11 basis points to 5.03%. Just last week, it traded at 5.36%. That is a sharp decline and, taken on its own, would normally be considered supportive for gold. The dollar's message is less clear. The greenback is lower against the JPY, CHF and CAD, but higher against the EUR, GBP, AUD and NZD. So the double tailwind is not fully in place. Nevertheless, with yields falling sharply, traders might reasonably have expected gold to find buyers. Instead, gold is down around $60 and has traded to its lowest level since August. That is where the technicals become useful.

For background, Canada's producer price data come in two monthly reports from Statistics Canada: the Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI) and the Raw Materials Price Index (RMPI). They're typically released together at 8:30 am ET, a few weeks after the reference month ends. The IPPI measures prices that Canadian manufacturers receive for goods as they leave the factory gate, covering everything from refined petroleum and lumber to metals, chemicals, food products and motor vehicles. The RMPI tracks the prices manufacturers pay for raw materials, including crude oil, metal ores, logs, grains and livestock. Many of those inputs aren't produced in Canada, so the RMPI is effectively a gauge of global commodity costs flowing into Canadian industry. The headline figures are the monthly and annual changes in each index, and neither is seasonally adjusted.

title: Market playbook: Why a convincing market story doesn't always make a good trade
body: If you've been in markets long enough, I'll bet you have surely encountered a situation where you were absolutely sure that something was going to happen. And as it turned out, you called it and you were right. But somehow, you still ended up losing money on the trade. Does that sound familiar? Well, I would say it's one of the biggest traps that a trader can fall into. It is the very fact that even having a convincing market story doesn't necessarily mean you have a good trade. Let's go back to our little apple store example, shall we? Just imagine that you are selling apples and one day, you hear that bad weather has damaged apple harvests across the country. With that information, you quickly make the connection that supplies are going to fall and apple prices should go up because of that. Hence, you decide to stock up on apples at $2 each, hoping to sell them for $3 later. That sounds like a decent business opportunity, no? But then, here's the catch though. You're not the only person with this information. Everyone else has heard about the bad weather too and other sellers have already rushed to buy apples, pushing the price from $1 to $2 before you even had a chance to get in on the action. And by the time you do and when the shortage does hit, apple prices only go up from $2 to $2.05. You were right about the shortage. You were even right that prices did go higher.

title: Why following crypto ETF flows is like looking in the rear-view mirror
body: Crypto ETF flows have become a popular indicator for gauging institutional demand. Strong inflows are often interpreted as bullish, while sustained outflows are seen as a warning sign. However, ETF flows tell you what investors have already done, not what they are likely to do next. By the time large inflows appear in the data, prices may have already rallied on the news that attracted investors. Similarly, outflows often accelerate after a selloff has begun. Traders who rely solely on these figures risk buying near the top or selling near the bottom, becoming the bagholders of a move that has already played out. Instead of waiting for ETF data to confirm a trend, traders should focus on what could trigger the next change in demand. For example, a softer than expected US inflation report could lead markets to price in a more dovish Federal Reserve, lower yields and easier financial conditions. This could encourage investors to increase their crypto allocations. Rather than waiting for ETF inflows to appear in the data, traders can immediately start to position for the expected increase. The same goes for ETF outflows. Rising geopolitical tensions, persistent inflation or deteriorating growth can weigh on risk sentiment and outflows as investors reduce risk. Focusing on what actually drives ETF flows allows a trader to anticipate changes in investor behaviour. Of course, the relationship is not always straightforward.

The costs are so staggaringly high and it's so crowded that would-be lenders are tapped out and the broader investing public is skeptical of piling into a crowded trade. It's now abundantly clear that much of the USD outperformance in the past year has been money flowing towards the US capex buildout and associated equities. If you wanted to invest in AI, the USA was the only real game in town. Now with valuations stretched and some questions about how the frontier models will compete with open source models, the economics of it all are in question. That's leading to a reverse of the same flows that drove the USD higher. Moreover, the fundamentals don't support the US dollar at current levels in a world that's seeing trading relationships fray and the US stuck in a quagmire in Iran.

title: US treasury excels $26 billion of five-year tips at a high yield of 2.367%
body: The Treasury sold $26 billion of 5-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, with the following results: High yield: 2.367%. WI level at the time of the auction: 2.360%. Tail: 0.7 basis point vs the average of 0.2 basis point. Bid to cover: 2.41X vs the average of 2.52X. Directs: 32.4% vs the average of 23.0%. Indirects: 62.1% vs the average of 67.8%. Dealers: 5.5% vs the average of 9.2%. Auction grade: C− A somewhat softer auction overall. The Treasury needed to offer a yield 0.7 basis point above the WI level to get the issue sold, a larger tail than average. Bid to cover was also below average, while indirect bidders (foreign buyers) took a smaller share. The offset was strong direct demand (domestic buyers), which helped leave dealers with just 5.5% of the issue—well below average. So there were some positives underneath the headline, but the tail and softer overall bidding keep the grade below a C-. What are TIPS, and how do they work? TIPS provide investors with protection against inflation by adjusting the security's principal with the Consumer Price Index. When inflation rises, the principal increases. The coupon rate stays fixed, but the dollar interest payments increase as that rate is applied to a larger principal balance. Payments are made every six months. www.treasurydirect.gov For example, take $1,000 of principal with a hypothetical 2% coupon.

title: ECB's Panetta says rising yields a drag on growth, not a crisis, ahead of rate meeting
body: Panetta's remarks put the focus on sovereign spreads, especially French and Italian debt against German Bunds, as the market's main stress gauge in the euro zone. If US yields keep rising, the spillover he describes could push periphery spreads wider, a risk for Italian bonds given his own warning. For the euro, a growth gap that favours the US alongside higher US yields is a headwind, even with the ECB still facing inflation near double its target. Oil remains the swing factor: sustained high energy prices keep inflation pressure on the ECB, while the drag from tighter financial conditions points the other way. That tension is likely to shape how markets read next week's decision. - With policymakers in their pre-meeting quiet period, Panetta's warning on bond yields is a reminder that markets may already be doing some of the ECB's tightening for it. Summary: Bank of Italy Governor Fabio Panetta said the rise in bond yields will weigh on the euro zone economy but is not critical at this stage. He described the bond sell-off as global and led by the US, where growth and inflation have beaten expectations, while European growth is weaker. Panetta pointed to France's high debt and deficits as a source of pressure, said Germany's stronger finances have limited its yield rise, and noted spillovers to Italian borrowing costs. title: Trump invokes Defense Production Act for oil as pump prices bite 12 days before midterms
body: The memo does little to change the near-term oil balance, which is still driven by the Iran conflict. Brent closed around $113 on Thursday, its highest since early May, after reports that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. That geopolitical risk premium outweighs any supply response the Defense Production Act can deliver in the coming weeks. The measure is more relevant for refining margins and US refiners: federal financial support for capacity could, over time, ease tight diesel and gasoline cracks that have pushed pump prices above what crude alone implies. Traders are also likely to watch for further pre-election steps aimed at fuel costs, which could add headline volatility to US product futures even if their physical impact is limited. --- With fuel costs at record seasonal highs and the midterms less than two weeks away, the White House is again using a Korean War-era law to boost oil supply, though any relief at the pump will take longer than the campaign. Summary: President Trump signed a memo determining that domestic petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense. The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, which allows federal financial support, purchases and purchase commitments to expand capacity. It builds on an April determination covering petroleum and recent steps, including a Defense Production Act-backed expansion of a Delek refinery in Texas.

title: OpenAI close to raising up to $30 billion at $1.25 trillion valuation, UAE investors lead
body: The round gives listed markets a fresh read on how private investors are pricing frontier AI after recent volatility in AI-linked shares. A valuation below the roughly $1.4 trillion OpenAI had sought could be read as a sign of greater price discipline. That reading would matter for chipmakers such as Nvidia and for infrastructure names tied to AI capital spending. SoftBank, a major existing OpenAI investor, is among the most direct listed proxies, and its Tokyo-traded shares may respond to any new mark on the stake. The size of Gulf participation also shows how much of the AI buildout depends on sovereign capital, which ties the sector more closely to oil revenues and Middle East geopolitics. --- Earlier: Nasdaq sinks as chip stocks tumble --- CNBC (may be gated) report. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round. The reported valuation is notably lower than the figure OpenAI had been seeking earlier this month. Bloomberg reported in early October that the company was looking to raise at least $30 billion at a pre-money valuation of about $1.4 trillion. According to that report, OpenAI was presenting the valuation to prospective investors as a fixed price, even though it had not yet chosen a lead investor. That approach is unusual for a private round, where investors would normally propose and negotiate terms. Gulf money has been central to the talks from the start.
